description:
Rizal was also a sculptor of small animals, an “animalier”, fashionable in Europe in the 19th century. He worked with plaster, clay and bakawan paste. While in Dapitan, he collected specimens of insects and small animals and shipped these to Mr. A.B. Meyer, a German ethnologist, in exchange for books. In letters to his family, he said he had shot so many wild boars (jabali) that he was tired of pork.

Dapitan, 14 March 1895

My Dear and Esteemed Friend,

Your letter of 15 December arrived here some days ago and I see that in spite of my good will the remittances do not arrive as they should. The head of the wild boar is a genuine head of wild boar. You will see that there is no ground to doubt it. However, one ought to note that between the wild boars and the domesticated hogs that are found here very little difference can be distinguished that would place the question in doubt. Either the wild boars of this country are no more than the domesticated hogs that have reverted to savagery or the domesticated hogs are nothing more than domesticated wild boars. These are the questions that can very well be asked. The wild boars that come every night to eat my coconuts differ little from those that I have at home. The only difference lies in the color, the leanness, the length of the canine teeth, and the hair.”

Rizal eventually created a clay sculpture of the jabali, which his sister, Narcisa Rizal, inherited. A sculptural reproduction by renowned sculptors Inocencio Gallemit and Alberto Cabardo, Jr. was later donated by Trinidad Rizal to the Bureau of Public Libraries in 1948. It has the same “Rizal Dapitan” inscription and is mounted on a stand with a brass plate that reads “wild boar.” The reproduction is currently on display in the Silid Pamana of the Museo ni Jose Rizal in Fort Santiago.
